title: Forward defence in depth: how to preserve Australia’s strategy of denial | The Strategist
paragraphs: Australia’s strategy of denial requires the Australian Defence Force to have the means to reduce an adversary’s confidence that force or coercion against this country can achieve its political and strategic objectives. However, the ADF’s ability to realistically achieve that objective is under increasing challenge by China’s continued, rapid and non-transparent military modernisation.

The Chinese armed forces now have the means to threaten Australian territory, deployed ADF units and critical national infrastructure through long-range strike, space, cyber and expanded power-projection capabilities. They can project naval and air power into Australia’s approaches and threaten the critical maritime trade routes and undersea infrastructure on which Australia’s security and prosperity depend. The growing reality that many of the capabilities being acquired by China could be employed beyond the effective reach of an ADF operating from northern Australia is of key importance for Australia’s approach to denial.

In an ASPI report published today, Projecting power forward: Strengthening Australia’s strategy of denial, I propose an operational concept of ‘forward defence in depth’. This concept involves investment and credibility in capability, across all five operational domains (land, sea, air, cyber and space), in partnership with the US and other allies and partners.
